title: Sikhism: honest work

cards: A holy man comes to town. Two invitations arrive. One is from the richest official in the district, throwing a lavish feast in his honor.
The other is from a poor carpenter with only coarse bread to offer. Which would you accept? The feast has the better food, the better company, the better look.
The holy man was Guru Nanak, and he went to the carpenter's.

teach.b: The story comes from the janamsakhis, the traditional life stories of Guru Nanak, and Sikhs tell it often. The carpenter was Bhai Lalo.

The rich man, Malik Bhago, was offended and demanded to know why the Guru had refused his feast. So, the story goes, Guru Nanak took Lalo's dry bread in one hand and Bhago's rich food in the other, and squeezed.

teach.h: MILK FROM ONE, BLOOD FROM THE OTHER.
teach.b: From Lalo's bread came milk. From Bhago's came blood. One had been earned by honest labor; the other squeezed out of the poor.
That's the heart of kirat karni: earning your living by honest work. Kirat means work, labor; karni means doing. It's the second of the three pillars Guru Nanak taught, after remembering the name.
And it pushes against a familiar picture of holiness: leaving work behind to live on alms.

In a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib, at Ang 1245, he criticizes those who call themselves holy while begging at other people's doors, and praises the one who eats what he earns by his own effort and gives some away.
That person, he says, recognizes the path.
Sikh tradition says he lived it: in the last years of his life he settled at Kartarpur, on the bank of the Ravi, and farmed, working the fields alongside the community.

For Sikhs, honest work isn't a distraction from the spiritual life; it's part of it. No cheating, no exploiting, no living off others when you can work, and the name remembered while the hands are busy.

how: Sikhs are taught to earn their living through honest work in any trade or profession, avoiding exploitation and begging, and to keep remembering the name while they work.

o: a vow of hard labor done as a penance
doing unpaid service at the gurdwara
earning a living honestly, without exploiting

s: Guru Nanak taught that a holy life means leaving work to live on alms
he praised the one who eats what he earns and gives some away.
Guru Nanak farmed at Kartarpur in his last years
he worked the fields alongside the community.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak. a rich official invites you to a feast; a poor carpenter offers coarse bread. whose invitation do you accept?
games.why: in the janamsakhi story he stays with Bhai Lalo, and squeezes milk from his bread and blood from Bhago's feast.

practice: Picture the work in front of you today, paid or unpaid: a job, a class, a household, caring for someone.
Ask quietly whether you're cutting a corner, bending the truth, taking credit, or leaning on someone else's effort; no guilt, just notice. Then choose one piece of it to do fully and cleanly.

wordCard.voice: Kirat karni. Earning your living by honest work: the second pillar of Sikh life, lived by Guru Nanak in the fields at Kartarpur. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: honest work. Bread like Lalo's, earned with your own hands. Day two hundred seventy-six.
